title: the dice game
hook: Duryodhana and Shakuni work on the blind king, a hall is built for the game, and Vidura's warning goes unheeded
carry: let a worry change one thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dice game was born on the road: Duryodhana's envy, and Shakuni's plan to win without a war. Your line was name the sting before it becomes a plan. Did you name a sting before it became a plan? Day seven hundred sixty-six.

A plan needs permission. Duryodhana is a prince, not the king. To invite Yudhishthira to anything, the invitation has to come from his father, Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura. So uncle and nephew go to the palace. Shakuni speaks first, gently, about how pale and thin the prince has grown. And the king, who loves his son, asks him what's wrong. Today the plan moves from a road to a throne room, and we watch a father decide.
screen: `A PLAN NEEDS PERMISSION.` → `TO THE BLIND KING.` → `A FATHER ASKS WHAT'S WRONG.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana tells his father what he told Shakuni: the Pandavas' wealth, the kings at their feet, the hall that shamed him. And Shakuni lays out the game. Dhritarashtra hesitates. In the telling, he says he wants to ask Vidura first, his wise half-brother, whose counsel he trusts. And Duryodhana pushes back hard. If you ask Vidura, he says, in effect, Vidura will stop it, and I'll be lost. He presses until his father gives way. So the king orders a new hall built for the game, a splendid one, worthy of the guests. Only then does he call Vidura, not to ask whether, but to tell him. And Vidura says plainly that he doesn't approve. This game, he warns, will set the cousins against each other. It will end in quarrel. Dhritarashtra listens, and doesn't change course. He answers that if the gods are kind, no harm will come; that what is fated will happen. And then he gives Vidura a job. Go to Indraprastha, he tells him. Bring Yudhishthira here to play. Look at what's happened. The one man who sees the danger clearly is the one sent to deliver the invitation. A father who couldn't say no to his son has made the counselor he trusts most the messenger of the thing he warned against. The poem doesn't call Dhritarashtra wicked. It shows a man who heard the warning, and loved his son too much to act on it.
screen: `DHRITARASHTRA HESITATES.` · `DURYODHANA PUSHES PAST VIDURA.` · `A HALL IS BUILT FOR THE GAME.` · `VIDURA WARNS, AND IS SENT ANYWAY.` · then, large: `HE HEARD THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders loosen, and the hands rest. Bring to mind a time you said yes to someone you love when part of you wanted to say no: a child, a partner, a parent, a friend. Picture the moment you gave way. What made the yes easier than the no? There's no grade here. Just see it clearly. Breathe in, and let the memory be what it was. Breathe out, and notice whether a no would have been a kind of care too. If you pray, you can bring that yes, and that person, to your prayer. If not, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Vidura. The counselor who warns that this game will end in quarrel, and is sent anyway, by the father who couldn't refuse his son, to carry the invitation he spoke against.
Your line: let a worry change one thing. Today, when someone you trust raises a worry, let it change one thing before you go ahead. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: In Hindu retellings, Vidura is remembered as a voice of wise counsel at the Kuru court, the one who tells the blind king what he doesn't want to hear.

fork.setup: you're Dhritarashtra. the counselor you trust has just told you the game will end in quarrel. your son is desperate. what do you do?
options: send the counselor to invite Yudhishthira.
ask the elders for a vote.
fork.reveal: he says that what is fated will happen, and sends Vidura himself to Indraprastha with the invitation.

original.note: Sanskrit vidura: the name of Dhritarashtra's half-brother, the counselor who warns against the game.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dice game was the Pandavas' choice.
what it means: it was set up in Hastinapura, approved by a father who couldn't refuse his son, against Vidura's warning.
what a scholar hears: Dhritarashtra answers a clear warning by appealing to fate, which lets him go ahead without owning the choice.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Shakuni and Duryodhana persuade Dhritarashtra; the hall built; Vidura's warning; Vidura sent to invite Yudhishthira)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Shakuni speaks of Duryodhana's pallor; Dhritarashtra wishes to consult Vidura first; Duryodhana objects that Vidura will dissuade him (Ganguli also has him threaten his own life; omitted here).
Confirm the order: the hall is ordered built before Vidura is told, and Vidura's warning is about dissension among the sons.
Confirm Dhritarashtra's reply appeals to the gods and to fate, and that he sends Vidura to Indraprastha to invite Yudhishthira.
Trapdoor third floor: 'a move the poem returns to at many hard turns' is a general claim about the poem; a Keeper may soften or cut.
The game itself and Yudhishthira's response to the invitation are left for day 767.
